# Introduction

## Outline

* P1: Immunomodulatory receptors are key therapeutic targets but generate limiting off-target effects.
    + Molecules that interact with surface receptors are the largest class of therapeutics.
    + Immunomodulatory receptors often dictate immune cell function and are thus involved in a broad range of immune-mediated diseases.
    + Two properties of immune receptors:
        * Shared receptor expression across cells of different functions leads to off-target binding
        * Cellular pleiotropy leads to counteractive signals in off-target cells
    + Combined, these features lead to off-target binding which produces signals that counteract the desired effect (at best) and generate severe adverse effects (at worst)
    + Immunomodulatory ligands are rarely adopted because of severe adverse effects that arise from off-target binding.
* P2: Protein engineering efforts have reduced off-target binding through avidity-dependent targeting.
    + The promise of immunomodulatory molecules has spurred extensive protein engineering efforts aimed at reducing off-target binding
    + Chief among these are multivalent, affinity-engineered cytokine muteins fused to targeted antibody scaffolds (targeted, multispecific cytokine fusions) 
    + Coordinated changes in affinity and valency allow these molecules to preferentially bind target cells despite modest differences in receptor expression between target and off-target populations.
    + These molecules owe this so-called cell-type selectivity to avidity effects wherein low-affinity, multivalent molecules require high receptor density to bind effectively
* P3: Often, binding is all that matters.
    + Multispecific molecules with decoupled signaling and targeting domains have been shown to further enhance cell-type selectivity
    + In these cases, high-affinity and/or high-valency targeting subunits direct signal domain binding toward target cells, while low-affinity signal domains are unable to bind off-target cells despite high signal receptor density
    + Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates use targeting domains to direct cytotoxic payloads based on surface protein expression
    + Considering only the targeting function of surface proteins reveals a vast number of potential surface targets which might be exploited alone or in combination.
* P4: Combinatorial complexity has left the development of multispecific, targeted therapeutics unguided.
    + Evolution has granted us with thousands of unique surface proteins
    + These proteins may, in some combination, facilitate perfectly selective delivery of signal to any given cell type
    + However, the number of possible combinations of surface proteins is combinatorially large
    + This complexity has left the field of multispecificity unguided and siloed.
    + Even systematic explorations neglect to comprehensively evaluate the selectivity of the large space of possible targets, especially across different target cell types
* P5: Here, we use a high-throughput computational platform to systematically explore the multi-receptor targeting space and identify key properties of multispecificity.

## Body

Immunomodulatory receptors dictate cellular activity by binding their cognate ligands. In concert, these interactions drive most immune functions, making immune receptors key therapeutic targets for a number of disease indications. However, attempts to control immune function by administering immunomodulatory proteins have broadly resulted in dose-limiting toxicities as a result of two phenomena. First, immune receptors are seldom solely expressed on cells of a single function---distinct cell types often express similar amounts and types of immune receptors. Second, the signal generated upon binding these receptors is heavily influenced by cellular context. In combination, these properties expose the observed limitation: upon administration, a protein will bind its cognate receptor expressed on target and off-target cells and elicit distinct, often counterproductive, responses from each cell type. The key challenge with immunomodulatory proteins is therefore enforcing cell-type selectivity, or the propensity to preferentially bind target cells over off-target populations.

Significant progress has been made to this end by way of protein engineering. Three arms of engineering have proven especially fruitful in the niche of immunomodulation and immunotherapy: (1) affinity engineering, (2) valency engineering, and (3) antibody fusion.

Chief among these advances are multivalent, affinity-engineered cytokine muteins fused to targeted antibody scaffolds (targeted, multispecific cytokine fusions).
